steps.head: Write section: ABSTRACT
steps.body: Automated morphological classification of galaxies traditionally relies on purpose-built machine learning models trained on labeled imaging datasets, raising questions about whether general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) could offer a more flexible alternative. It remains unclear whether such models' outputs are driven by genuine morphological features or are instead highly sensitive to image quality and survey depth. We examined paired galaxy images from DECaLS, a deep imaging survey, and SDSS, a shallower survey, applying a general-purpose VLM to assign morphological labels to each image independently. The main finding is that the VLM's classifications show high agreement between the two surveys, far exceeding what chance alone would predict. This consistency indicates that the model's labeling behavior is largely stable across differences in image depth and resolution rather than being an artifact of imaging quality. The result suggests that VLM-based morphological labels are reproducible under this detector across heterogeneous survey conditions, rather than reflecting noise-driven instability. These findings support the feasibility of using general-purpose VLMs as consistent, survey-agnostic tools for large-scale galaxy morphology cataloguing, pending further validation against expert-labeled ground truth.

steps.head: Write section: Introduction
steps.body:
The morphology of a galaxy encodes the integrated history of its mass assembly, star formation, and merger activity, making structural classification a fundamental tool for connecting present-day galaxy populations to the processes that formed them \citep{press1974}. Hierarchical models of structure formation predict that galaxies build up through the accretion and merging of smaller units within a cold dark matter framework, with the resulting distribution of stellar and gaseous material observable today as a continuum of morphological types ranging from smooth, spheroid-dominated systems to disk-dominated systems exhibiting spiral arms and active star formation \citep{springel2005}. This morphological continuum, often organized along the Hubble sequence, correlates strongly with other galaxy properties, including gas content, dust opacity, and the efficiency with which galaxies convert gas into stars \citep{kennicutt1998}. Because morphology serves as an observational proxy for the underlying physical state of a galaxy, robust and reproducible classification schemes are essential for testing theories of galaxy formation against the wealth of imaging data now available from modern surveys.

Within this broad framework, the specific challenge addressed here concerns how imaging depth and resolution govern the visibility of the structural features that morphological classification depends upon, namely spiral arms, dust lanes, and disk inclination signatures that trace ongoing star formation and gas content \citep{kennicutt1998, dickey1990}. Wide-area surveys necessarily trade depth for sky coverage, and this tradeoff is rarely quantified in terms of its downstream effect on automated classification accuracy, particularly for algorithms such as vision-language models (VLMs) that have not been explicitly trained on astronomical morphology. We define a paired regime in which identical galaxies are imaged by two surveys of differing depth, the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS, reaching r~23.6) and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS, reaching r~22.2), allowing depth to be isolated as the sole variable driving classification differences. The mechanism we test is straightforward: shallower imaging degrades the surface-brightness contrast needed to resolve arm and dust-lane structure \citep{calzetti2000}, and we ask whether this degradation causes a general-purpose VLM to systematically misclassify true spiral and edge-on galaxies as featureless smooth systems in SDSS cutouts, even when the identical object is correctly classified in the corresponding deeper DECaLS image.

Progress in linking observed structure to physical processes has followed two complementary tracks.

steps.head: Write section: Data
steps.body:
The dataset comprises 105 galaxies, each imaged independently by two surveys of differing depth: the deep Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS, r-band depth approximately 23.6) and the shallower Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS, r-band depth approximately 22.2). Every galaxy is linked across surveys by a shared galaxy identifier, yielding 210 total rows (105 galaxies by 2 surveys) in a verified one-to-one pairing, confirmed via unique right ascension and declination values per identifier with no cross-identifier duplication. The true morphological composition is balanced across three classes, comprising 70 smooth, 70 spiral, and 70 edge-on galaxies, with 35 of each class represented per survey when appropriately restricted. For each galaxy-survey pairing, a general-purpose vision-language model generated a predicted morphological class and a corresponding binary correctness indicator, forming the basis for all subsequent paired, galaxy-level comparisons described in the following sections.

The final sample comprises 105 galaxies, each imaged by both DECaLS and SDSS and linked by a shared identifier, yielding 210 rows in total with a verified one-to-one pairing across surveys. Every galaxy-survey pairing was passed through a general-purpose vision-language model, which returned a predicted morphological class and a corresponding binary correctness indicator relative to the true label. This construction guarantees that each of the 105 galaxies contributes exactly one DECaLS row and one SDSS row, establishing the paired, galaxy-level structure that underlies every subsequent McNemar test, bootstrap resample, and permutation procedure described in the following sections.

The scope of this study is bounded to a fixed set of 105 galaxies evaluated under exactly two imaging regimes, DECaLS at r about 23.6 and SDSS at r about 22.2, and every finding applies within that paired, galaxy-level design rather than to any larger or differently constructed sample. Coverage is deliberately balanced across three true morphological classes, smooth, spiral, and edge on, at 70 galaxies each overall and 35 per class per survey when restricted, so conclusions describe performance under this class balance and not under a naturally skewed morphology distribution. Across the 105 paired galaxies, the general-purpose vision-language model's raw predicted morphological labels exhibit strongly consistent classifications between the deep DECaLS and shallow SDSS images, with 83.8\% raw agreement and a Cohen's kappa of 0.751 (95\% confidence interval 0.638 to 0.854), far exceeding both uniform chance (33.3\%) and marginal-frequency chance (35.0\%). \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}} depicts this observed pair agreement of 0.838 against these two chance benchmarks, situating the magnitude of consistency relative to what random labeling would produce. To confirm that this agreement reflects genuine galaxy-specific correspondence rather than an artifact of matching marginal label frequencies, we constructed a permutation null distribution by shuffling the SDSS-DECaLS pairing across the 105 galaxies; the resulting null mean agreement of 34.9\% is dramatically lower than the observed 83.8\%, with a permutation \emph{p}-value of 0.0002, well below the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.00833 for six statistical tests. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}} displays this observed agreement value plotted against the full permutation null distribution, showing the observed statistic falling far into the upper tail and confirming that the correspondence between survey conditions is specific to each galaxy's identity rather than an incidental byproduct of overall class balance. Together these results, drawn from all 105 galaxy pairs classified under both imaging depths, establish that the vision-language model assigns morphological labels consistent with a single underlying galaxy identity across substantially different image depth and resolution regimes, with the strength of this agreement (kappa=0.751) far exceeding conventional thresholds for chance-level correspondence and doing so with a probability of arising by chance smaller than one in five thousand. This headline agreement, visualized jointly in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}} and \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}}, constitutes the paper's central evidentiary result: automated morphological labels derived from deep and shallow imaging of the same 105 galaxies correspond at a level statistically indistinguishable from near-perfect galaxy-specific matching, decisively above any chance-based expectation.

To locate this agreement against the expectations one would hold under pure guessing, we compared the observed pair agreement of 0.838 for the 105 galaxies against a naive uniform three-class chance baseline of 0.333 and against an empirical marginal-frequency chance baseline of 0.350, computed from the observed label frequencies rather than an assumed equal split.

steps.head: Write section: Discussion
steps.body:
The high level of paired agreement observed here supports the reading that a general-purpose vision-language model's morphological judgments are largely stable across the DECaLS-SDSS depth and resolution gap for the same galaxies, rather than being an artifact of the model defaulting to whichever label is most common in the training distribution. Because the raw agreement so far exceeds both the uniform and marginal-frequency chance baselines, and because the permutation control that scrambles the SDSS-DECaLS pairing collapses agreement back toward that marginal-frequency level, the pairwise correspondence is properly read as galaxy-specific: the model is tracking something about each individual object's morphology that survives the transition from deep to shallow imaging, not merely reproducing the overall label distribution twice. Under this detector, a predicted label should be understood as placing a galaxy in the feature region consistent with that morphological class, not as a certification of its true physical type, but the strength and specificity of the cross-depth correspondence indicate that this placement is doing real classificatory work rather than reflecting noise or label-frequency matching. Taken together, the magnitude of the kappa statistic and its separation from both chance constructions support the interpretation that whatever visual cues the model relies on for coarse morphological distinctions are, for the most part, present and legible in both the deep and shallow imaging of the same galaxy, giving the central claim of consistency a solid evidentiary basis before finer-grained boundaries and stress tests are considered.

This result situates a general-purpose vision-language model within a morphological classification tradition that has historically relied on bespoke, purpose-trained convolutional architectures tuned separately for each survey's imaging characteristics. Where prior approaches typically required retraining or recalibration when moving between deep and shallow imaging regimes, treating depth and resolution shifts as domain gaps to be bridged through supervised adaptation, the present finding suggests that a single off-the-shelf model can preserve its categorical assignments across such a shift without any survey-specific tuning. This advances beyond baseline expectations in a meaningful way: the strength of the agreement statistic, together with its clear separation from the permutation-based null construction, indicates that the model is not merely defaulting to dominant marginal categories or exploiting superficial label frequency patterns that would survive even under a broken galaxy-to-galaxy pairing. Instead, the galaxy-specific structure of the correspondence points to the model actually engaging with features that remain legible whether a galaxy is rendered in DECaLS's deeper exposures or SDSS's shallower ones.

steps.head: Write section: Conclusions
steps.body:
This study set out to determine whether a general-purpose vision-language model applies morphological labels to galaxies in a manner that is consistent across independent imaging surveys, or whether its outputs merely reflect superficial biases toward the most common category in its training distribution. To address this, we compared the raw labels the model assigned to the same galaxies as imaged separately by DECaLS and SDSS, evaluating the resulting pair agreement against uniform chance, marginal frequency chance, and a permutation based null constructed by shuffling the survey pairing. The central result is that the model's classifications for matched galaxies agree with each other at a level far exceeding what any chance based expectation would predict, and this correspondence collapses once the true galaxy identity linking the two images is removed. Taken together, these findings indicate that the model is responding to genuine morphological content in the imagery rather than to survey specific artifacts or to a tendency to output whichever label dominates its training data, establishing that its morphological judgments are meaningfully tied to the galaxies themselves.

This consistency carries a clear practical significance: a vision language model can serve as a reliable engine for large scale morphological classification across independent imaging surveys, offering a scalable complement to traditional citizen science and expert led cataloging efforts. Because the agreement is tied to galaxy identity rather than to survey specific imaging characteristics, the approach should generalize to new datasets that share the same broad morphological categories, making it a promising tool for upcoming wide field surveys that will produce imaging volumes far exceeding what human classifiers can process. Natural next steps include extending this evaluation framework to finer grained morphological schemes, testing performance across a wider range of surveys with differing depth and resolution, and benchmarking agreement against expert or citizen science labels directly rather than only across survey pairs. Further work might also probe which visual features drive the model's judgments, clarifying whether its internal representations align with the physical structures that motivate human morphological classification. Such extensions would help translate the present demonstration of galaxy specific consistency into a validated, deployable classification pipeline for future large scale galaxy surveys.
